title: Ballast Weather
passage:
Jointed track opened a gap at every fishplate each summer; welded rail has no such luxury. It has nowhere to put the extra millimetres, so what would have been movement becomes force, and whether the force goes anywhere is settled by stone: the ballast packed between the sleepers and, above all, the shoulder heaped beyond their ends. A tamping machine lifts the track and packs new stone underneath, and for a few weeks afterwards that stone is loose. Twenty-seven degrees is the stress-free temperature in Isak Vessholm's district; it tells him how hard a July afternoon will push against the rail, and nothing about what is resisting it. His log runs to 39 buckles – track shoved sideways out of line – across 19 summers, and two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work. The hottest week on record produced none. Gangs are sent wherever somebody has reported something, Vessholm says, so the quieter miles go uncounted.
– Esme Quillenby

questions.prompt: What are we told about the buckles in Vessholm's log?

options.text: That a gang usually turned up to work the ballast within weeks of one appearing.
That two thirds of them came soon after a gang had worked the ballast.
That they all fell in the eight weeks following a tamping machine's visit.
That most of them fell in the hottest weeks the district has on record.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail: the key paraphrases the log's own tally. The passage states that Vessholm's log 'runs to 39 buckles ... across 19 summers, and two in three came in the eight weeks after ballast work'; B recasts that as two thirds arriving soon after a gang had worked the ballast, which is what the record says and nothing more. The passage has already supplied the mechanism that makes the timing legible – welded rail 'has nowhere to put the extra millimetres', so the force is held or not held by stone, and a tamping machine 'lifts the track and packs new stone underneath, and for a few weeks afterwards that stone is loose' – so a reader can both retrieve the detail and see why it is the interesting one. A = reversed order (reversed causality): it inverts the arrow, putting the gang's ballast work AFTER the buckle instead of before it, and it is tempting because the closing sentence does have gangs being sent wherever somebody has reported something. But that sentence is about which stretches enter the log at all – the point it makes is that 'the quieter miles go uncounted' – and it never says a reported buckle brings ballast work; the tally sentence fixes the order explicitly the other way round ('in the eight weeks after ballast work'). C = quantifier_upgrade: 'two in three' absolutised to 'they all', with the passage's own eight-week window and its tamping machine kept in place so that the option reads like a faithful summary. A third of the logged buckles fell outside that window, which is precisely the proportion the passage is careful to state. D = outside_knowledge plus the intuition a reader brings to the topic – heat buckles rails, so the hottest weeks should hold the most buckles – which the passage contradicts in one flat sentence: 'The hottest week on record produced none.' D also mis-hears the twenty-seven-degree stress-free figure, which the text says tells Vessholm how hard a July afternoon will push against the rail and 'nothing about what is resisting it'. Hedge balance: the key is the specific, unhedged claim; the two hedged options ('usually' in A, 'most' in D) are both wrong and the single hard absolutiser ('all', in C) sits on a distractor, so neither 'pick the qualified answer' nor 'strip the absolutes' locates the key. Lengths under mech tokenization: key B 14 words against A 15 / C 14 / D 14, so the key is joint-shortest rather than longest (ratio 1.07, cap 2.36).
